comments.author: pqpdf
comments.text: Hi HN, I'm the author of PQCrypta Proxy. It's a Layer-7 reverse proxy written in Rust with HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC, WebTransport, CONNECT-UDP, JA3/JA4 fingerprinting, and hybrid post-quantum TLS support. We currently use it in front of all PQ Crypta production services, including pqcrypta.com, the HTTP/3 analyzer, the PQC readiness scanner, speed test infrastructure, PQ PDF, and our authoritative DNS services. Building and operating it in production led us to discover a number of interoperability and standards-compliance issues in HTTP/3, QUIC, DNS, and post-quantum deployments, some of which are documented on our site. One thing I'm looking for is feedback from people operating Nginx, Caddy, Traefik, Envoy, HAProxy, or Cloudflare-based stacks. What would make you consider a new Rust proxy, and what would immediately stop you from deploying one? Happy to answer questions.

comments.author: ivraatiems
comments.text: I just don't see this as deadly to the production of games the way others do. GTA 6 is a monumental human achievement in video games - in fact it's arguably one of the largest artistic endeavors ever undertaken. If numbers are to believed, it has also already made around $4 billion against a $1-2 billion budget. It is massively profitable, and doubtless will become more so as DLC and a real PC port are released. It's deeply frustrating that everyone else will get to experience it before me because I didn't want to spend hundreds of dollars on a console! comments.author: Tiberium
comments.text: For the general picture: the Xbox version of the game was leaked by Cyberleek - first the resources, then the game binary. Because modern Xbox is very close to a Windows PC with some extra Xbox stuff, running the actual game code isn't hard, it's mostly about compatibility and graphics, plus the binary doesn't have any special DRM/obfuscation. The current projects (xcl and VIctory) basically take a Wine-like approach. The main problems they have to solve, as I understand: - The game ships with raw RDNA 2 shaders, so the projects have to translate that to another format, e.g. DXIL for DirectX 12, and compile those shaders. So you need a good translation/recompilation pipeline, if it's bad, the shaders will be bloated and perform poorly - Xbox has unified memory, while most PCs do not, so you have to add a lot of workarounds and book-keeping for the game to work properly with that - Xbox's DirectX 12 differs from the normal Windows one in some ways, and the game uses Xbox-specific texture formats with DirectStorage I just wanted to share this because there's a lot of misconceptions going around about this being a "recomp" or something like that. Decompiling the entire binary (it's about 100MB of real executable machine code) will be a much bigger effort than getting this binary to run.

comments.text: While this does largely work, there are a few complications. The biggest one being power management, especially the cutting off of power to a specific port. If a host wants to cut off power to a 3.x device, it typically needs to know which 2.x port that device is connected to. The host internally can have some really wild mappings of 2.0 and 3.x hubs, controllers, etc, but the device tree or ACPI tables let it know exactly which ones are paired together for any port leaving the device. After that point it is assumed that the host can learn the topology from any hubs attached. The power management is tied to the 2.0 port. Unexpectedly splitting the topology could lead the host to instruct a hub to cut off power to the wrong port when trying to target a specific USB 3.x device. Also, if a hub indicates that a device is drawing excessive current, and there is nothing communicating on the 2.0 lines, there is a risk of the wrong 3.x getting blamed by the host, possibly showing a warning popup to the user with the wrong device name, or similar. This isn't to say this is always a problem, because it isn't but it is something to be aware of.

What would be possible with a circular (thus omnidirectional) simple data plug (with a few pins as possible) given modern tech?

comments.author: Lerc
comments.text: A LLM should be considered an advisor to the same extent as legal, financial, and medical. They should be legally required to act to the best of their capability in the interests of their client, subject to the same requirements that they don't break the law to do so as applies to legal, financial, or medical advisors. An important part of that is that they must never represent themselves as acting for someone who is not their client. This still allows them to work for you while being the client of their parent companies, but it would disallow claiming to be serving a client when that person is not their client. When an AI says it is serving your best interests, it must actually be doing so. The nature of client confidentiality is that it exists because in order to advise appropriately, a full understanding of the client's situation might be necessary. The legal protection of confidentiality enables disclosing the required information without fear of making it public. That too should be protected with AI in your service. All of this is established principle. I don't see any reason why this should not be applied to AI as well. The same principles have the same reasoning as the current legally protected advisors. This is an absolute must for the common benefit to society. The alternative is a world where people increasingly trust the ever-more-reasonable sounding AIs while the answer to the question "Who should I vote for?" is available to the highest bidder.

comments.author: jpatten
comments.text: I find the argument here pretty flimsy. The author is upset that Claude respects Bandcamp's wish to not make its site accessible to LLMs? Clearly the alternative is worse. It seems the outcome in the post is more a result of the usage policies of the sites in question, rather than the fault of the LLM or its creator. I'm not claiming these AI companies are somehow incapable of wrongdoing. We've already seen a lot of dubious behavior and I'm sure we'll see a lot more. But I do think these companies owe it to their investors and to society to try to put reasonable guardrails around how their products are used. We shouldn't fault them for doing so.

comments.author: jgrahamc
comments.text: > One of my biggest problems with this is the fact that Cloudflare doesn't do enough to notify website administrators about these issues. I think we made a very large effort to make sure our customers were using TLS to the origin. In 2022, we released the SSL/TLS Recommender ( https://blog.cloudflare.com/ssl-tls-recommender ) which helps a customer figure out what settings they can use for their origin connection. This is a bigger deal than you might think at Cloudflare scale because end customers aren't always in control of their TLS configuration on their server (e.g. imagine they are using a WordPress hosting company). In 2024, we had confidence that at scale the recommender worked and announced we were going to automatically set the TLS level for origin connections ( https://blog.cloudflare.com/introducing-automatic-ssl-tls-se... ). In 2025, we followed up on that with a review of how that roll out had gone and announced post-quantum origin connections ( https://blog.cloudflare.com/automatically-secure ). Doing something at Cloudflare scale is always... weird. For example, we'd see situations where a customer had configured HTTP to their origin and if we switched to HTTPS automatically we'd get different content! You can read about those issues in this 2020 research paper: https://www.cs.umd.edu/~dml/papers/https_tma20.pdf

comments.author: derf_
comments.text: It is surprisingly easy to get unexpected negative values with floating point operations. One I remember was a square root that was failing on a negative argument despite that argument being clamped against zero . The problem was that the clamp was using some macros #define MIN(a, b) ((a) < (b) ? (a) : (b)) #define MAX(a, b) ((a) < (b) ? (b) : (a)) and the arguments were being clamped with MAX(x, 0). Well, if x is negative zero , it is not less than 0, so the macro returns x. The square root then looks at the sign bit and fails. Negative zero is a perfectly possible result from a series of calculations that destructively cancel.
